activities.anchor: The century of motivation research tells one long story
activities.caption: line up the motivation theories in time
activities.name: poTheoryOrder

config.prompt: A century of motivation research — order the theories as they arrived:
items: Taylor's scientific management (1911) — pay by the piece
Maslow's hierarchy of needs — a satisfied need stops motivating
Herzberg's two-factor theory — hygiene versus motivators
Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory, popularised by Pink — autonomy, mastery, purpose
config.why: The long story: money matters and it is not enough — each theory moved the levers further from the payslip and into the design of the work.

activities.caption: one line of the incentives story is wrong
activities.name: poIncentiveSpot

config.prompt: One line of this incentives summary is wrong. Find it.
lines: Self-determination theory: autonomy, mastery and purpose drive the best work
Extrinsic rewards can crowd out intrinsic motivation
Haifa day-care centres introduced a small fine for late child-pickup
Lateness fell sharply — the fine strengthened the moral obligation
Wells Fargo's quotas produced roughly 3.5 million unauthorised accounts — the metric, not the intent, was rewarded
config.correction: Lateness increased — the fine converted a moral obligation into a purchasable price.
config.why: Incentives work, often too well: reward the outcome you want, audit every outcome you did not list, and remember Goodhart's law.

activities.anchor: Two further frameworks earn their place
activities.caption: pair each job characteristic with its question
activities.name: poJobMatch

config.prompt: Hackman and Oldham's five job characteristics — pair each with the question it asks:

pairs.right: do I complete a whole, visible piece?
do I have discretion over how?

config.why: Vroom's version multiplies: effort × expectancy × instrumentality × valence — a zero anywhere zeroes the whole, so the unmotivated employee usually isn't lazy; a link is broken.

activities.anchor: The theory cashes out as a menu of non-financial redesigns
activities.caption: file each redesign by what it adds
activities.name: poRedesignBuckets

config.prompt: Four non-financial redesigns — file each by what it changes:

items.label: job enlargement — more tasks at the same level
job enrichment — add planning, deciding and checking

config.why: Match the mechanism to the deficit the diagnosis found, not the fashionable one — piece rates where quality matters more than quantity are corrosive.

activities.anchor: Structure is the organisation's answer to
activities.caption: place each decision — centre or edge
activities.name: poStructureBranch

config.root: Structure is who decides what, with whose information? Place each call.

start.text: Pricing for one regional customer. Central or edge?

choices.label: Centralise
choices.feedback: Consistent but blind to local reality — decentralise where local information matters.

choices.label: Decentralise
choices.feedback: Local reality decides — and a manager develops at the edge.

d1.text: Brand standards for the logo. Central or edge?

choices.label: Centralise
choices.feedback: Standards compound at the centre — brand, security and data belong there.

choices.label: Decentralise
choices.feedback: Every region its own logo — the brand dissolves.

c1.text: A crisis breaks at 2 a.m. Who decides the response?

choices.label: The top — decide and instruct
choices.feedback: Right in fires: centralised decisions are consistent and fast in a crisis — autocratic is right in fires, corrosive as a steady state.

choices.label: Consult the whole team first
choices.feedback: Slower consensus while the fire spreads — crises want the top.

c2.text: The centre keeps the compounding assets; the edge keeps the local ones.

c3.text: Crisis handled — now return the dial toward the edge, because most real firms oscillate.

d2.text: Reconsider — consistency is the point of a standard.

d3.text: Reconsider — a burning crisis is where the spectrum's autocratic end earns its keep.

config.why: Delegation passes authority down with the responsibility to match — delegating work without authority just creates frustrated errand-runners.

activities.anchor: is where the evidence is unambiguous
activities.caption: rank the selection methods by predictive power
activities.name: poSelectionOrder

config.prompt: Decades of meta-analysis rank the predictors — strongest first:
items: Work samples — do a slice of the actual job
Structured interviews — same questions, scored rubrics, past behaviour
Unstructured conversations — predict charm and similarity
Years of experience and unproctored references — barely beat chance
config.why: Structure strips the noise — interviewer mood, rapport, halo effects — that unstructured formats mistake for signal.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the training ladder
activities.name: poTrainingCloze

config.text: Training takes over: %%0%% (the first weeks, when most avoidable attrition happens), on-the-job training (cheap, contextual, riskier for customers) and off-the-job training (courses and simulations). And 'we train them and they might leave' is answered by 'what if you don't train them and they %%1%%?'
config.hint: One word names the first weeks; one word completes the retort.

activities.caption: true or false — the bloodstream's blockages
activities.name: poCommJudge

statements.s: Upward communication is the direction most organisations starve, because bad news must climb a hierarchy that punishes messengers.
statements.why: Formal channels that are slow are why classic bureaucracies become rumour engines.

statements.s: The grapevine is faster than official channels — and inaccurate in exact proportion to how little official communication exists.
statements.why: The informal network feeds on silence.

statements.s: Communication is complete when the message is sent.
statements.why: It is complete when the receiver's understanding is verified — feedback loops are the fix for overload.

statements.s: Sensitive news is best delivered by email so a record exists.
statements.why: Channel mismatch: sensitive news in person, complex nuance in writing.
